WHAT SCRIPTURE SAYS
What Scripture says of him

"King Agrippa and Bernice came unto Caesarea to salute Festus." Festus laid Paul's case before him: a man "left in bonds by Felix", accused over questions "of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive". Acts 25:13–19
Agrippa said, "I would also hear the man myself." Acts 25:22

Next day Agrippa and Bernice came "with great pomp" into the place of hearing. Festus said he had "no certain thing to write unto my lord" and had brought Paul "specially before thee, O king Agrippa". Acts 25:23–26

"Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Thou art permitted to speak for thyself." Paul called himself happy to answer before him, "because I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews". Acts 26:1–3

Paul told of his life as a Pharisee, his persecuting, the light and voice on the road to Damascus, and his preaching; he said, "the king knoweth of these things ... for this thing was not done in a corner." Acts 26:4–26
"King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest. Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." Acts 26:27–28

Rising with the governor and Bernice, they agreed, "This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds", and Agrippa said to Festus, "This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar." Acts 26:30–32

Scholars' viewSchürer (1890): through the war of 66–70 he stood on the Roman side; he hosted Vespasian at Caesarea Philippi and was with Titus.[13]

SCHÜRER (1890)

King of Chalcis from about AD 50; of Philip's former tetrarchy from AD 53, with parts of Galilee and Perea added by Nero; died in the third year of Trajan, AD 100, by the report of Justus of Tiberias preserved by Photius.
Almost persuaded, and in earnest
the KJV's rendering, following Chrysostom; J. A. Bengel (1742); John Gill (1746–1748); Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871)

They read the words as a real admission that Paul had nearly won him; Bengel sees "a motion towards good in him", and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown argue that Paul's reply ("both almost, and altogether") suits only that sense. Acts 26:28–29 [26][28][33]
"With little persuasion": a dismissive answer
H. A. W. Meyer (English 1877–1879); C. J. Ellicott's commentary (about 1880); J. R. Lumby (1882)

They hold that the Greek means "with little" (effort, words or time), not "almost", and read the reply as mockery: Ellicott calls it "a cynical sneer", and Lumby cites the Revised Version's "With but little persuasion thou wouldest fain make me a Christian". Acts 26:28 [22][3][27]

WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Acts never calls him Herod, and does not say whose son he was.
Acts does not say how Bernice was related to him.
Acts records his words to Paul but says nothing of his faith beyond them.
IDENTIFICATIONS THIS PAGE RELIES ON

From the textActs calls him "king Agrippa" and sets him beside Bernice in the time of the governor Festus. Acts never calls him Herod and does not say who his father was. Acts 25:13 Acts 25:23 Acts 26:30
Scholars' viewSchürer (1890) places the visit of Acts 25:13 in AD 60, when Agrippa and Bernice came "with great pomp" to welcome the new procurator Festus. Acts 25:13 Acts 25:23 [13]
